profile.behavior: Active foliage gleaner that hops and flits through outer leaves and slender branches, usually high in the canopy, taking caterpillars and other invertebrates. It often joins mixed-species foraging flocks outside the breeding season and may also eat fruit and nectar.
field_marks: Small, compact body with a short tail
Gray-olive head with a pale eyebrow and dark eye
Olive to yellow-green back and wings with weak or absent wingbars
White undertail coverts contrasting with dusky legs and tail
profile.habitat: Breeds in young or middle-aged boreal coniferous and mixed forests, especially areas with openings, dense shrubs, or boggy ground. During migration it uses many wooded habitats, groves, and brush; in winter it occupies open or semiopen tropical broadleaf and second-growth forests, including shade-grown plantations.

findings: The candidate depicts Tennessee Warbler accurately as a small, compact, short-tailed warbler with a thin, sharply pointed bill.

The primary specimen's gray-olive head, pale supercilium, dark eye, olive to yellow-green upperparts, weak or absent wingbars, plain pale underparts, and white undertail coverts agree with the licensed reference photographs and direct identification sources.
Plumage falls within documented variation for the species; the evidence does not require adding a seasonal, age, or sex qualifier.
The primary specimen has one head, one beak, one tail, a convincing pair of legs and functional gripping feet, and a plausible wing pair with the far-side wing naturally occluded by the lateral pose.

Both bill renderings have coherent shared bases, tapered mandibles, and pointed, non-truncated tips consistent with the clearest side-profile references; neither rendering shows a material projection reversal or inconsistency.
The detached wing and head are clearly supplementary studies rather than extra birds or parts attached to the primary specimen, and both are anatomically plausible.
The common name, scientific name, and family are correctly written and independently supported.

All visible measurement text matches the directly supported All About Birds measurement set: length 10–13 cm (3.9–5.1 in), weight 8–10 g (0.3 oz), and wingspan 19–20 cm (7.5–7.9 in), with the stated both-sexes qualifier.

The length diagram is internally consistent: 10 cm (3.9 in) is at the bottom, 13 cm (5.1 in) is at the top, the vertical range label agrees, and the diagram is explicitly marked SCHEMATIC — NOT TO SCALE.
The habitat, behavior, and all six field-mark lines are complete, legible, sensical, and match the proposed wording without a material omission, substitution, duplication, or numerical error.
The layout reads clearly as a scientific field-journal plate, with a dominant specimen, separated supplementary studies, coherent annotations, and no harmful overlap.
No map, coordinates, ZIP code, observation locality, or other local-observation detail appears; Tennessee occurs only as part of the species' established common name.
